body.text: Australian shares are set to open lower after Wall Street wavered, with Nvidia shares plunging following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang.
His departure follows revelations of two alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
Meanwhile, Microsoft platforms, including Outlook, has been hit by a widespread outage.

NAB needs to be 'match fit'
In his opening statement, NAB CEO Andrew Irvine has discussed three key things:
• Getting busted for underpaying 66,000 workers for more than a decade
Mr Irvine discussed the hard call to sack about 2,500 workers, saying NAB needs to be "match fit" as an institution.

"These were very difficult decisions … our approach is that every colleague needs to be treated with care, dignity and with respect."These changes will better position NAB (for the future)."I repeat that there will be no material impact on customer-facing banking roles."
"These were very difficult decisions … our approach is that every colleague needs to be treated with care, dignity and with respect.
"These changes will better position NAB (for the future).
"I repeat that there will be no material impact on customer-facing banking roles."
He went on to discuss AI, which he says "will be as consequential to how we live and work as any previous industrial revolution".
Was also keen to emphasise: "Recent workforce changes were not driven by AI."
He's now starting to talk about the court enforceable undertaking about under-paying staff.
They've paid back about $170 million and a $2 million fine.
"Paying our people correctly is non-negotiable," he notes.

Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, cut his price target on Nvidia shares from $US300 to $US225 on the anticipation of Jensen Huang's exit from the company.
Wall Street closes lower as Nvidia sell-off weighs on markets
Wall Street finished in the red, although the losses were relatively modest considering the turmoil surrounding Nvidia.
The chipmaker's shares plunged 14% at one point, although it managed to recover some losses by the close.

Retail investors were buying the dip, snapping up around $US111 million worth of Nvidia shares in the first 30 minutes of trading, the biggest opening buying spree on record for the stock, according to Vanda Analytics.
Here's how Wall Street finished:
The selling also spread to other AI-linked companies, with Nebius, CoreWeave and several data centre stocks coming under pressure.
But it wasn't all bad news for tech. Nvidia rivals AMD and Broadcom gained ground, while energy stocks were the standout performers on the S&P 500.
Markets are also now fully pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike of at least 25 basis points in December, according to CME FedWatch.
Prominent Wall Street tech bull slashes Nvidia's price target
Even before Jensen Huang's departure was confirmed, one of Wall Street's most prominent tech bulls was already preparing for life at Nvidia without him.
Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, cut his price target on Nvidia shares from $US300 to $US225 as he anticipated Huang’s removal as CEO.
"We also believe the old Jensen with the black leather jacket, Godfather, AI visionary viewed as a rock star globally is over and in the past."
Ives described the scandal as a dark day for Nvidia and a major blow to Huang's legacy, arguing that the board needed to move quickly to find a replacement.
But despite the turmoil, he's sticking with his outperform rating.

"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone."
He's also tipped Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress as a potential successor, while floating Apple's Tim Cook as a possible outside contender.
Nvidia scandal reaches the White House as Commerce Secretary faces questions over his future
Reuters is reporting that senior officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Lutnick has been facing growing criticism over the Trump administration’s handling of AI chip exports to China, with lawmakers questioning why dozens of Chinese companies haven’t been added to a key US trade blacklist.
The US has not added any companies to that list since October 2025, which is the longest gap in more than a decade.
The criticism began well before Huang's resignation, but the scandal has brought fresh scrutiny to Washington's oversight of advanced chip exports to China.
Earlier on Thursday, a White House official said President Donald Trump maintained complete confidence in Lutnick.
ICYMI: ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland on its action against two banks this week

The corporate regulator has taken action against two banks in two days. ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland told Alicia Barry this should send a signal to banks that they need to get the "basics right" for customers.
Key Event
Jensen Huang steps down, Nvidia shares plunge by as much as 14%
If you're just catching up on the news this morning, Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia after two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company says finance chief Colette Kress will step in to serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is found. The company will consider internal and external candidates as part of that search.
The board has also appointed longtime director Harvey Jones to become its first ever chair.
Huang, who owns 3.61% stake in the company, will also leave the board.
Nvidia's shares plunged at the market open, tumbling by 14%, before paring losses to finish down about 5%. Retail investors are taking the opportunity to buy the dip.

Huang wasn’t just the boss of Nvidia. He was seen by many as the face of the AI boom. The leather jacket became his trademark, and his appearances at tech conferences around the world often felt more like rock concerts.
He co-founded Nvidia and helped build it into one of the world’s most valuable companies, leaving behind a tall task for the board to find his permanent successor.
